comparison: Both evaluate statistical analysis claims (C40-C43). OpenEval finds the approach rigorous and appropriate with sound pre-specification of tests. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, questioning whether ANOVA assumptions are met and suggesting alternative tests (contrasts within ANOVA, non-parametric tests), indicating the proposed analysis may need revision.

Both address power calculations (C45-C47, C65-C70). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to impossible 282.39% power value, estimation errors from figure extraction, and potentially inflated effect sizes. Peer reviewers also express uncertainty, noting power calculations were based on t-test and suggesting they may need revision based on alternative statistical approaches.

Both evaluate the original study methodology and rationale (C2, C8-C12). OpenEval finds claims accurate and logically sound but notes the underlying assumption isn't critically evaluated. Peer reviewers support these claims, acknowledging the study context and replication rationale without raising concerns.

Both address project structure claims (C1, C6, C7). OpenEval finds these descriptive claims consistent and supported. Peer reviewers also support these claims as part of accepting the overall study context and background without critique.

Both evaluate methodological details (C21-C30, C52-C57). OpenEval finds comprehensive methods internally consistent and following standard protocols. Peer reviewers implicitly support these technical procedures, focusing critiques elsewhere rather than questioning these methodological claims.

Both address experimental design details (C27, C60-C64). OpenEval supports the comprehensive methodological details as internally consistent. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, explicitly questioning the 11 vs 12 day duration and why cohort 2 has only 5 mice versus 14 in other cohorts, requesting justification for these design choices.

Both evaluate original study results and cell line limitations (C14-C16). OpenEval supports the data extraction and notes C16's valid limitation acknowledgment. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about generalizability from a single cell line, noting drug activity is 'highly idiosyncratic' and most journals require multiple cell lines/models.

Both address experimental limitations (C16). OpenEval supports the limitation acknowledgment as valid given single cell line design. Peer reviewers express stronger uncertainty, explicitly questioning the limitation of using only A549 cells and noting requirements for multiple models.

Both evaluate cimetidine mechanism claims (C3, C13). OpenEval identifies critical pharmacological error (C3 incorrectly states agonist while C13 correctly states blocker) and rates UNSUPPORTED. Peer reviewers support these claims without challenge, accepting the background information about cimetidine.

Both address data extraction from original study (C35-C39, C58-C59). OpenEval supports the specific quantitative data extraction as consistent. Peer reviewers also support these claims, not questioning the accuracy of extracted data or effect size calculations.

Both evaluate supporting studies (C18-C19). OpenEval supports these as providing convergent evidence while noting they use different systems. Peer reviewers accept these background claims without challenge, focusing critiques on experimental design rather than prior findings.

Both address data sharing and meta-analytic plans (C34, C44). OpenEval supports the clear data sharing plan and appropriate meta-analytic approach. Peer reviewers also support these aspects, not raising concerns about data sharing or meta-analysis methods.

Both evaluate protocol differences (C31-C33). OpenEval supports transparent documentation while noting substantial injection volume difference. Peer reviewers implicitly support these methodological details, not raising concerns about the documented protocol deviations.

Both address data extraction and effect size calculations (C71-C73). OpenEval expresses uncertainty due to estimation errors from figures and SEM-to-SD conversion compounding errors. Peer reviewers support the accuracy of extracted values, not questioning the data extraction methods.

Both evaluate original study results (C4-C5). OpenEval supports the consistent description with quantitative data. Peer reviewers also support these claims about the original findings without challenge.
